title: Type Class
body:
A named set of operations that a type may declare it supports. [[Parametric Polymorphism]]
gives you one implementation that works for *every* type by knowing nothing about it; a type
class is the other kind, **ad-hoc polymorphism**, where behaviour differs per type and you say
so explicitly.

```haskell
class Eq a where
    (==) :: a -> a -> Bool

instance Eq Colour where
    Red   == Red   = True
    Green == Green = True
    Blue  == Blue  = True
    _     == _     = False
```

The class declares the signature, the `instance` supplies the code for one type. A function may
then demand the capability in its signature:

```haskell
elem' :: Eq a => a -> [a] -> Bool      -- "for any a that has an Eq instance"
```

Everything left of `=>` is a **constraint**. `Eq a => a -> [a] -> Bool` is still one
implementation for all types, but only types that can be compared are allowed in.

## The standard ladder

Worth knowing by name, because the whole library is organised around them:

| Class | Key operation | Means |
|---|---|---|
| `Eq` | `==` | can be compared for equality |
| `Ord` | `<=` | can be ordered; requires `Eq` |
| `Show` | `show` | can be printed |
| `Read` | `read` | can be parsed from a string |
| `Num` | `+`, `*` | is numeric |
| [[Functor]] | `fmap` | can be mapped over |
| `Applicative` | `<*>` | can apply a wrapped function |
| [[Monad]] | `>>=` | can be sequenced |

`Ord` requiring `Eq` is a **superclass** constraint, and the last three are a genuine hierarchy:
every monad is an applicative and every applicative is a functor. That ladder is the spine of
[[Monad]].

## Against OO interfaces

The obvious comparison, and the differences are the interesting part:

| | [[Interface]] (Java) | Type class |
|---|---|---|
| Declared | in the class definition | separately, any time |
| Retrofittable | no: you cannot make a library type implement your interface | yes: write an instance for a type you did not author |
| Dispatch | at run time, on the object, see [[Polymorphism]] | at compile time, on the type |
| Can constrain a return type | no: `create() -> T` cannot dispatch on what you want back | yes: `read :: Read a => String -> a` |
| Runtime cost | a vtable lookup | none; the instance is chosen and passed statically |

Rows two and four are the ones that are not just phrasing. Retrofitting means the "I cannot make
`String` implement my interface" problem does not exist. And return-type dispatch is impossible
in Java by construction: `read "42" :: Int` and `read "42" :: Double` call different code
chosen by what the caller wants, and no method-on-an-object can do that because there is no
object to dispatch on yet.

The cost is the mirror image: an instance is chosen at compile time, so you cannot put values of
different types in one list and let them behave differently, which is the everyday Java move.
The type class answer to that is a heterogeneous wrapper, and it is deliberately more effort
than the [[Polymorphism|OO]] version, because it is deliberately rarer.

## Deriving

Instances for the obvious classes are mechanical, so the compiler will write them:

```haskell
data Colour = Red | Green | Blue deriving (Eq, Ord, Show)
```

`Ord` here orders by constructor position, `Show` prints the constructor name. See
[[Algebraic Data Type]] for the definitions this attaches to.

## Core Facts to Know

- A type class is a set of operations a type declares it supports.
- `class` declares the signatures; `instance` supplies the code for one type.
- This is **ad-hoc** polymorphism: different code per type, chosen by type.
- [[Parametric Polymorphism]] is the other kind: one code path for all types.
- `Eq a => ...` is a **constraint**; everything left of `=>` is a requirement on the caller.
- A class may require another (`Ord` requires `Eq`): a superclass constraint.
- [[Functor]] → `Applicative` → [[Monad]] is a real hierarchy, each requiring the last.
- Unlike an [[Interface]], instances are retrofittable onto types you did not write.
- Unlike an interface, dispatch can be on the **return** type: `read :: Read a => String -> a`.
- Dispatch is resolved at compile time, so there is no vtable and no run-time cost.
- `deriving (Eq, Ord, Show)` has the compiler write the mechanical instances.
